what: Colossus Mark 1, a programmable (plugs and switches) electronic valve machine, performed satisfactorily at Dollis Hill (GPO research station, London) under Tommy Flowers.

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: It performed satisfactorily at Dollis Hill on 8 December 1943

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: Colossus is regarded as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer.

note: Earlier candidates: Atanasoff-Berry computer (tested 1942) is electronic but not programmable; Zuse Z3 (May 1941) is programmable but electromechanical relays. Later and stricter readings: ENIAC (general-purpose, Dec 1945 / dedicated Feb 1946) and Manchester Baby (first stored-program, 21 June 1948). Colossus is not stored-program and was special-purpose, so fit to 'stores data and runs programs' is partial. The first pass (ENIAC 1945) was later.

what: Colossus Mark 1, installed at Bletchley Park, attacked its first Lorenz-cipher message (processing intercepted traffic for the Allies).

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: It was operational in January and it successfully attacked its first message on 5 February 1944.

note: Delivered to Bletchley 18 Jan 1944 and operational that month; first real message 5 Feb 1944. Rejected as earlier: ABC (never used for real work). ENIAC's first real program (Dec 1945) is later.

what: Sir William Thomson's tide-predicting machine (built 1872-73 by Alexander Legé, with Edward Roberts); a model was exhibited at the British Association meeting, 1873.

sources.title: Tide-predicting machine
sources.quote: A model of it was exhibited at the British Association meeting in 1873

note: Judged on mechanism: continuous mechanical quantities (pulleys and cranks) summing harmonic terms, i.e. it models an equation, but it evaluates a fixed formula rather than solving general equations. If the definition is read strictly as 'solves differential equations', the earliest working machine is Bush's MIT differential analyzer (1928-31, first pass), with Hartree's Manchester model 1934. James Thomson's 1876 integrating machine was a description, not a working solver. Rejected as loose analogues: planimeters, astrolabe and the Antikythera mechanism (c.150-100 BC, an orrery, not an equation solver).

what: A larger tide-predicting machine (20 components) was built for the Government of India and used to generate tide data for Indian ports.

sources.title: Tide-predicting machine
sources.quote: An enlarged and improved version of the machine, for computing 20 tidal components, was built for the Government of India in 1879

note: The 1876 ten-component machine may have produced earlier tide tables but no use date was found. Arthur Pollen's naval fire-control analog computer (c.1912) and Bush's differential analyzer (1931, used operationally in the 1930s) are later.

what: Herman Hollerith's first tabulators compiled mortality statistics for Baltimore, Jersey City and New York City (trial of the card-and-counter system).

sources.title: Tabulating machine
sources.quote: Hollerith's first tabulators were used to compile mortality statistics for Baltimore, Jersey City and New York City in 1886.

note: Wikipedia says 1886; other histories (Smithsonian, Franklin Institute, USPTO, per search summaries I could not fetch) put the Baltimore trial in 1887, so the date may be 1887. Hollerith's patent application was filed 1884 but described a concept. Earlier punched-card machines (Jacquard 1804, Korsakov 1832 proposal) do not tabulate, count or sort records, so were rejected.

what: Hollerith electric tabulators compiled the 1890 US Census from about 100 million punched cards.

sources.title: Tabulating machine
sources.quote: Hollerith's method was used for the 1890 census.

note: The 1886/87 Baltimore mortality work was a trial; the 1890 census was the first large-scale official deployment. If the mortality compilation is counted as real use, the date would be 1886-87.

what: The Banu Musa brothers in Baghdad described an automatic flute player driven by a pinned barrel, in their Book of Ingenious Devices (c. 850).

sources.title: Banu Musa
sources.quote: credited with inventing the first music sequencer, as described in the manuscript, as an example of an early type of programmable machine.

sources.title: Banu Musa
sources.quote: a Persian family of polymaths, astronomers, mathematicians, and engineers active in 9th century Baghdad

note: Date is approximate (the book is conventionally dated c. 850; the page says only 9th century). Pinned-barrel machine plays a recorded sequence without an operator, so mechanism fits, though the page hedges ('may have been the first programmable machine'). Earlier: Hellenistic automata (e.g. Hero) not checked. The first pass (1952 MIT numerical control) and Jacquard 1804 are later.

what: Basile Bouchon, a silk-weaving worker in Lyon, controlled a drawloom with a perforated paper roll.

sources.title: Basile Bouchon
sources.quote: invented a way to control a loom with a perforated paper roll in 1725

sources.title: Basile Bouchon
sources.quote: This development is considered to be the first industrial application of a semi-automated machine.

note: Bouchon's loom still needed an extra operator, so it is only partly 'rather than by an operator'. Falcon 1728, Vaucanson 1745 and Jacquard (patent 1804, 'wildly successful' 1805) refined it; Jacquard is the first fully card-driven loom in wide use. Musical automata with pinned barrels (c. 850 on) were pleasure devices, not production use.

what: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated the first working integrated circuit (germanium, wire-bonded).

sources.title: Integrated circuit
sources.quote: successfully demonstrating the first working example of an integrated circuit on 12 September 1958

sources.title: Q80831
sources.quote: time of discovery or invention (P575): 1958

note: Earlier ideas considered: Jacobi's 1949 patent and Dummer's 1952 concept (concepts, no working circuit found); micromodules (1957) were assembled discrete parts. Noyce's monolithic planar IC followed about six months later.

what: Integrated circuits entered use in products and in the US space and military programs; NASA's Apollo program was the largest single consumer 1961-65.

sources.title: Integrated circuit
sources.quote: NASA's Apollo Program was the largest single consumer of integrated circuits between 1961 and 1965.

note: Date is inferred from the start of the 1961-65 consumption window; I did not confirm the first commercial IC sale (Texas Instruments/Fairchild, c. 1960-61), which may be slightly earlier. No earlier use of Kilby's 1958 prototype found.

what: General Electric built a demonstration computer from thin-film cryotrons (arrays of 2000 devices operated), following John Bremer's 1957 planar cryotron.

sources.title: Cryotron
sources.quote: In the next few years, a demonstration computer was made and arrays with 2000 devices operated.

note: The page gives only 'the next few years' after 1957, so the year 1960 is approximate (1958-1961). Buck's 1953-55 cryotron was a single switching element, not a computer. No machine described as a working superconducting computer was found in other sources. No practical use: cryotron work was abandoned by the mid-1960s and, per Wikipedia, there are no commercial superconducting computers as of 2016. No mass adoption.

what: Valdemar Poulsen invented the Telegraphone, the first magnetic recorder (steel wire); he demonstrated it at the 1900 Paris Exposition.

sources.title: Wire recording
sources.quote: The first crude magnetic recorder was invented in 1898 by Valdemar Poulsen.

note: Earlier: Oberlin Smith's 1888 Electrical World article proposed wire recording but no working machine is recorded. The definition includes sound, so the audio telegraphone counts. Later: tape 1928 (Pfleumer), drum 1932 (Tauschek), RAMAC disk 1956 (first pass).

what: The American Telegraphone Company of Springfield, Massachusetts manufactured the Telegraphone, the first commercially available magnetic recorder, for dictation and telephone recording.

sources.title: Wire recording
sources.quote: manufactured by the American Telegraphone Company, Springfield, Massachusetts in 1903

note: Page says use was 'extremely limited' through the 1920s-30s. Earlier practical use (e.g. the 1900 Paris demonstration recording of Franz Josef) was a demonstration. Digital data use began later with UNIVAC I tape (1951) and RAMAC (1956). mass_adoption left out: the page says affordable tape recorders for home and office appeared in the first half of the 1950s but gives no firm year.

what: John Benjamin Dancer produced microphotographs (daguerreotype images reduced 160:1), viewed through a microscope.

sources.title: Microphotography
sources.quote: John Benjamin Dancer was one of the first to produce microphotographs, in 1839.

note: Dancer's work was a novelty with no document-storage purpose; the idea of microphotography for preserving documents was first suggested by Glaisher in 1851 and Herschel in 1853. Fit to 'books and records on film read through a viewer' is loose, as the first pass said. Rene Dagron's 1859 patent and Otlet's 1906 microphotographic book are later.

what: During the Siege of Paris, Rene Dagron microphotographed dispatches on thin collodion film; carried by pigeon, they were projected by magic lantern and transcribed.

sources.title: Microform
sources.quote: By 28 January 1871, when Paris and the Government of National Defense surrendered, Dagron had delivered 115,000 messages to Paris by carrier pigeon.

note: Earlier than the first pass (Recordak 1928, bank cheques; page says commercial use began in the 1920s with McCarthy's 1925 Checkograph). The pigeon-post films carried messages and newspaper pages, a close match to records on film read through a projector.

what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC (40 vacuum-tube neurons, Navy-funded) at Princeton; it learned to solve a maze.

sources.title: SNARC
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

sources.title: Marvin Minsky
sources.quote: In 1951, Minsky built SNARC, which is often considered the first artificial neural network.

note: Earlier than the first pass (Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58). McCulloch and Pitts (1943) was a non-learning mathematical model, not a built machine; Farley and Clark (1954) simulated a Hebbian network on a computer, later than SNARC. Exact month of SNARC working not found (funded summer 1951).

what: Bell Labs applied convolutional neural networks trained by backpropagation (LeNet) to handwritten digit recognition for zip codes, later reading cheques in ATMs.

sources.title: LeNet
sources.quote: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. at Bell Labs first applied the backpropagation algorithm to practical applications

note: Widrow and Hoff's ADALINE (1960) and MADALINE (largest built 1963) adaptive filters are described by Wikipedia as 'likely the first artificial neural network applied to a real-world problem' (phone-line echo removal), which would be earlier, but I found no dated first deployment. The CIA studied the Mark I Perceptron 1960-64 only as an evaluation.

what: Google Translate switched to the neural machine translation system GNMT in November 2016, putting neural networks in daily use by very large numbers of ordinary people.

sources.title: Google Neural Machine Translation
sources.quote: In November 2016, Google Neural Machine Translation system (GNMT) was introduced.

note: Year is a judgment: ordinary people used neural networks unknowingly earlier (cheque reading from the 1990s, speech recognition from the early 2010s) and no source states when use became routine.

what: Leonard Adleman (USC) solved a seven-node directed Hamiltonian path problem using DNA molecules in a test tube.

sources.title: DNA computing
sources.quote: Adleman demonstrated a proof-of-concept use of DNA as a form of computation which solved the seven-point Hamiltonian path problem.

sources.title: DNA computing
sources.quote: the field originally started with the demonstration of a computing application by Leonard Adleman in 1994

note: No earlier computation by living cells or organic chemistry in a deliberately built computer was found; later demonstrations include DNA walkers (2003) and 3-SAT with 20 variables (2002). Publication month (Science, Nov 1994) is from the first pass, not confirmed here. No practical use or mass adoption: still laboratory research.

what: Texas Instruments' 'Cal Tech' prototype, led by Jack Kilby, was the first handheld electronic calculator (paper-tape output).

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: The first handheld calculator was a 1967 prototype called Cal Tech

note: Earlier: the Curta (1947) was a mechanical, not electronic and not battery-powered. Desktop electronic calculators from 1961 (ANITA) were too big to be pocket devices. Wikidata gives only 'start time: 1960s' for 'calculator'.

what: The first commercially produced portable electronic calculators (Sanyo ICC-0081, Canon Pocketronic, Sharp QT-8B) appeared in Japan.

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: The first commercially produced portable calculators appeared in Japan in 1970

note: Earlier than the first pass (Bowmar 1971, HP-35 1972). Sharp EL-8 (Jan 1971) was close to pocket size. Exact 1970 month not given.

what: Pocket electronic calculators became popular as integrated circuits cut their size and cost.

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: They became popular in the mid-1970s as the incorporation of integrated circuits reduced their size and cost.

note: 'Mid-1970s' is the source's wording; 1975 is my choice of year.

what: John Blankenbaker designed the Kenbak-1, a TTL-logic 8-bit computer intended for individuals and schools.

sources.title: Kenbak-1
sources.quote: Designed in 1970 by John Blankenbaker

note: Date is the design year; no exact date of a working prototype was found. Rejected as earlier: Wikidata's 1957 (IBM 610 Auto-Point was single-operator but a costly office machine), LINC (1962, a laboratory minicomputer), Olivetti Programma 101 (1965, programmable calculator) and Datapoint 2200 (June 1970, a terminal). The Computer History Museum, per Wikipedia, calls the Kenbak-1 the first personal computer.

what: The Kenbak-1 went on sale in early 1971 at about $750 (fewer than 50 built).

sources.title: Kenbak-1
sources.quote: was first sold in early 1971

note: Earlier than the first pass (Altair 8800, Jan 1975). Micral N (early 1973) was the first microprocessor-based PC. Very few units sold, so use was marginal.

what: Psion launched the Organiser, a pocket computer with a one-line LCD and database; Wikipedia calls it the 'world's first practical pocket computer'.

sources.title: Psion Organiser
sources.quote: Launched in 1984,  the Psion Organiser was the "world's first practical pocket computer".

note: Same event as first_practical_use. Earlier candidates: Pitroda's 1975 electronic diary patent (no device found); Sharp PC-1211 pocket computer (March 1980, a programmable computer, not a notes/schedule device); Thorp and Shannon's 1961 shoe roulette computer (not a notes device). Organiser II (1986) is the first 'usable' PDA per Wikipedia.

what: Psion Organiser sold in the UK as a pocket diary and database computer.

sources.title: Personal digital assistant
sources.quote: The first PDA, the Organiser, was released in 1984 by Psion

note: Same date as demonstration; the Organiser I was a commercial product from the start.

what: Palm's PalmPilot handhelds (first Palm line March 1996, PalmPilot March 1997) reportedly sold over a million units by 1998.

sources.title: PalmPilot
sources.quote: PalmPilot had reportedly sold over 1 million units by 1998.

note: The page gives a sales figure rather than a 'became common' date, so 1998 is a judgment; Apple Newton (1993) sold poorly.

what: IBM presented the Naval Ordnance Research Calculator (NORC) to the US Navy; at the ceremony it calculated pi to 3,089 digits in 13 minutes.

sources.title: IBM NORC
sources.quote: At the presentation ceremony, it calculated pi to 3,089 digits, which was a record at the time.

note: NORC was 'likely the most powerful computer at the time' but is not usually called a supercomputer, so fit is uncertain. Later contenders: UNIVAC LARC (delivered June 1960), IBM 7030 Stretch (1961), Atlas (1962), CDC 6600 (1964, first pass 1965).

what: NORC moved to the Naval Proving Ground at Dahlgren, Virginia and was the main computer there (ballistics and ordnance calculations) until 1958.

sources.title: IBM NORC
sources.quote: In 1955, NORC was moved to the Naval Proving Ground at Dahlgren, Virginia. It was their main computer until 1958

note: It went into service December 1954 at the Watson laboratory; 1955 Dahlgren is the clear working deployment. LARC delivery to Livermore (June 1960) is later.

what: ENIAC was used for calculations of thermonuclear reactions for Los Alamos, its first program.

sources.title: ENIAC
sources.quote: In December 1945, the ENIAC was used to calculate thermonuclear reactions.

sources.title: Computer simulation
sources.quote: its first large-scale deployment during the Manhattan Project in World War II to model the process of nuclear detonation

note: Earlier than the first pass (ENIAC Monte Carlo, spring 1948, 'first fully automated Monte Carlo calculations'). Wikipedia dates the first large-scale computer simulation to the Manhattan Project (1944-45, by punched-card machines) but I did not confirm a date or a computer. Whether the Dec 1945 run counts as a model simulation rather than a calculation is a judgment; the 1944 Cambridge differential-analyzer simulations of transmission lines are not a first.

what: The same ENIAC run served Los Alamos hydrogen-bomb feasibility research.

sources.title: ENIAC
sources.quote: its first program was a study of the feasibility of the thermonuclear weapon

note: Same event as first_demonstration. Monte Carlo neutron-diffusion simulations followed in spring 1948 (Von Neumann, Metropolis).

what: GM Research's 'Digital Design' (later DAC-1) interactive graphics design system shown working at General Motors, 1959

sources.title: DAC-1
sources.quote: The system, known as Digital Design, was demonstrated and improved throughout 1959.

note: Rejected later candidates: DAC-1 full demo at IBM Kingston Dec 1962, Sketchpad (Sutherland, Jan 1963 report), DAC-1 public unveiling 1964; Hanratty's PRONTO (1957) is numerical-control programming, not interactive design by computer. The 1959 date rests on one Wikipedia statement and the early system's scope is unclear.

what: Production DAC-1 went live at GM in Warren, Michigan, used to design automobile parts (trunk lid modelled Nov 1963)

sources.title: DAC-1
sources.quote: The production DAC-1 system went live in Warren in April 1963.

note: Sketchpad (1963) was a thesis research system, not production. Earlier numerical-control tools (PRONTO 1957) are machining aids and were not counted. Not exhaustive for other countries (e.g. Citroen SPAC, Renault, 1960s).

what: Robot Scientist 'Adam' (Aberystwyth/Cambridge, Ross King) autonomously generated and tested hypotheses on yeast genes and found new knowledge

sources.title: Robot Scientist
sources.quote: Adam became the first machine in history to have discovered new scientific knowledge independently of its human creators.

note: Year 2009 (Science, 2 April 2009) is from memory/first pass: the pages I could reach (Wikipedia only) give no year. Earlier candidates: DENDRAL (1960s, Stanford; Wikipedia says it aimed to study hypothesis formation and discovery in science) and Meta-DENDRAL (mid-1970s, proposed new mass-spectrometry rules) are partial fits (analysis and rule induction but no experiments, human-directed) and I could not source dates. So earlier event may exist.

what: Test at Bedford, Massachusetts: radar data sent over telephone lines to a computer (Whirlwind), showing detection of a mock enemy aircraft; directed by C. Robert Wieser

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: data produced by a radar was transmitted through telephone lines to a computer for the first time, showing the detection of a mock enemy aircraft.

note: Earlier candidates: wartime radar/teleprinter links and Bell Labs relay computers remote-operated by teletype (1940 Complex Number Calculator demo, not checked here). Later: SAGE network 1958, SABRE 1960, CTSS 1961, ARPANET 1969. Chose 1951 test as first computer reached over lines from a distant sensor; not exhaustive.

what: SAGE New York sector became operational: computers linked by telephone/modem lines to radar sites and other centers in routine air defense

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: On "June 26, 1958,…the New York sector became operational"

note: Later: SABRE airline reservations 1960 (Wikipedia Computer network: 'In 1960, the commercial airline reservation system semi-automatic business research environment (SABRE) went online'), CTSS remote users. Pre-SAGE operational use (e.g. Cape Cod System tests from 1953, manual-era links) were tests, not service.

what: First ARPANET message UCLA to SRI (Wikidata inception of the Internet)
note: Only fits the network part of the definition (not worldwide, not for ordinary people). Considered: Minitel trial 15 July 1980 (national, terminals in homes), CompuServe/MicroNET consumer service 1979 (commercial online, not worldwide), WWW system working end of 1990. A stricter reading of the definition would put the demonstration around 1990-91.

what: The World (Brookline, MA) served its first customer, the first commercial Internet service provider offering the public direct access

sources.title: Internet service provider
sources.quote: Its first customer was served in November 1989.

note: Earlier home-terminal services (Minitel 1980-82 in France, CompuServe 1979) were not the Internet. Australian ISP also 1989.

what: Public use of the Internet and Web took off after NSFNET was decommissioned and traffic opened to commercial providers

sources.title: Internet
sources.quote: Since 1995, the Internet has tremendously impacted culture and commerce

note: Year is a judgement; the source supports 1995 as a turning point, not a user count. Adoption by ordinary households was later (2000s) in many countries.

what: First ARPANET network mail sent (Ray Tomlinson, BBN), introducing user@host addressing

sources.title: Email
sources.quote: In 1971 the first ARPANET network mail was sent, introducing the now-familiar address syntax with the '@' symbol

note: Wikidata gives invention 1971 as well. Mass adoption not sourced: Wikipedia only says email is ubiquitous, no date.

what: Lockheed completed the earliest form of Dialog under Roger K. Summit, an online interactive retrieval system

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

note: Earlier candidate: MEDLARS (NLM, 1964), a batch computer retrieval service, not interactive 'in seconds'; also pre-computer mechanical retrieval (Goldberg's Statistical Machine, 1931) rejected as not computerized.

what: MEDLINE, the online version of NLM's MEDLARS, became available for interactive searching from remote medical libraries

sources.title: MEDLINE
sources.quote: In late 1971, an online version called MEDLINE (MEDLARS Online) became available as a way to do online searching of MEDLARS from remote medical libraries.

note: Rejected earlier: MEDLARS 1964 (launched by NLM, 'first large-scale, computer-based, retrospective search service available to the general public') was a real service but batch-mode, so it does not meet 'in seconds'. Dialog commercial service started ~1972 (not sourced). If batch counts, practical use is 1964.

what: IBM Watson answered open-domain Jeopardy! clues in natural language and beat champions Rutter and Jennings (matches taped Jan 2011, broadcast Feb 2011)

sources.title: Watson (computer)
sources.quote: in 2011, the Watson computer system competed on Jeopardy! against champions Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings, winning the first-place prize of US$1 million.

note: Rejected earlier: BASEBALL (1961) and LUNAR (1971) answered questions only in narrow databases (Wikipedia: 'effective in their chosen domains'), so they do not match 'broad knowledge, arbitrary questions'; SHRDLU (blocks world) likewise. Web QA like Ask Jeeves (1997) matched questions to pages. Broad-domain systems may exist between 1990-2010 (e.g. START) which I could not source.

what: George Yevick and Adnan Wally invented an e-reader with a liquid-crystal display

sources.title: E-reader
sources.quote: The first e-reader was invented by George Yevick and Adnan Wally in 1972.

note: Source says invented and never commercialized; unclear whether a working unit was built. Dynabook (Kay, 1968-72) was a concept only.

what: Rocket eBook (NuvoMedia) went on sale in late 1998 as an early commercial handheld e-reader storing ten books; SoftBook and others appeared around 1998

sources.title: Rocket eBook
sources.quote: The Rocket eBook is an early commercial handheld e-reader that was produced by NuvoMedia in late 1998

note: Replaces the first-pass 2004 Sony Librie (first E Ink reader, not first reader). Sony Data Discman (1990) played CD-ROM books and is listed by Wikipedia among first commercial e-readers; not dated by a fetched source, so 1990 may be earlier. Mass adoption (Kindle, 2007; sold out in hours) left unsourced for a fetched page.

what: Nick Sheridon at Xerox PARC developed Gyricon, the first electronic paper (rotating two-color balls)

sources.title: Electronic paper
sources.quote: Electronic paper was first developed in the 1970s by Nick Sheridon at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center.

note: Source says only 1970s; 1974 or 1975 per first pass. Earlier rewritable displays (liquid crystal, electrophoretic displays of the 1970s by others) not examined.

what: Sony Librie in Japan, first e-book reader with an E Ink electronic paper display

sources.title: Electronic paper
sources.quote: In 2004, Sony released the Librié in Japan, the first e-book reader with an electronic paper E Ink display.

note: Possibly earlier: Gyricon and E Ink signage and electronic shelf labels around 1999-2003 (no fetched source; NCR electronic shelf labels 1997 used other display tech). Librie is the first source-confirmed consumer product.

what: First practical optical holograms recording 3D objects made by Denisyuk (USSR) and by Leith and Upatnieks (Michigan), viewable from several angles

sources.title: Holography
sources.quote: the first practical optical holograms that recorded 3D objects to be made in 1962 by Yuri Denisyuk in the Soviet Union

note: Static holograms are a loose match for a 'display'. Other candidates: 1966 varifocal-mirror volumetric display (Volumetric display page), 1972 moving white-light hologram (Lloyd Cross), 1989 MIT electroholographic video display. Perspecta (2001) rejected as late. Gabor 1947-48 holography produced no 3D display.

what: MIT Spatial Imaging Group pioneered electroholography, an electronically driven moving 3D holographic display

sources.title: Holographic display
sources.quote: 1989 – MIT spatial imaging group pioneered electroholography

note: This is a lab system, so really a second demonstration; no routine practical use of holographic displays found. Treat as low.

what: MIT Whirlwind computer solved an equation and displayed the solution on an oscilloscope (third quarter of 1949)

sources.title: Whirlwind I
sources.quote: In the third quarter of 1949, the computer was advanced enough to solve an equation and display its solution on an oscilloscope

note: Earlier: Manchester Baby (June 1948) and EDSAC (1949) had CRTs showing memory contents (Williams-tube monitors) but for engineers, not as output display; not counted.

what: Whirlwind became operational in 1951, real-time output on CRT displays used in Cape Cod radar tracking

sources.title: Whirlwind I
sources.quote: Operational in 1951, it was among the first digital electronic computers that operated in real-time for output

note: Display-specific operational use date is approximate; SAGE-like display uses (1951 Bedford test) are the same era.

what: Bedford, MA test: radar data sent by phone line to a computer, displaying a mock enemy aircraft detection (Whirlwind)

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: data produced by a radar was transmitted through telephone lines to a computer for the first time, showing the detection of a mock enemy aircraft.

note: Other candidates: DATAR (Royal Canadian Navy/Ferranti, trial late 1953 on Lake Ontario, displays on plan-position indicators), Cape Cod System tests from Sept 1953, Royal Navy CDS (analog, 1940s). 1951 is earliest found.

what: SAGE New York sector became operational, direction-center consoles showing radar tracks from the computer

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: On "June 26, 1958,…the New York sector became operational"

note: First pass said 1958-07-01 at McGuire AFB; fetched page gives 26 June 1958 for New York sector. DATAR was not fielded; CDS-based Royal Navy ADA later.

what: E. A. Johnson (Royal Radar Establishment, Malvern) published a finger-driven capacitive touchscreen for air traffic control

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: He described his work on capacitive touchscreens in a short article published in 1965

note: Earlier: AT&T Harmon 1962 patent for a light-beam stylus touchscreen (patent only, not shown working). Data gloves: Sayre Glove 1977, later. Light pens (1950s) are pointing devices, not touch.

what: CERN transparent capacitive touchscreen (Beck and Stumpe) put into use for the SPS control system

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: Manufactured by CERN and later by industry partners, it was put to use in 1973.

note: Also PLATO IV optical touch terminals (patent filed 1972) used in education; and Johnson's was used in air traffic control, unverified.

what: Touchscreen phones were rapidly gaining popularity by 2009 after the 2007 LG Prada and iPhone

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: By 2009, touchscreen-enabled phones were rapidly gaining popularity

note: Date is a judgement (2007-2010). iPhone announced Jan 2007; first-pass 2007 date replaced by when popularity is stated.

what: David Shepard and Harvey Cook built the 'Gismo' reading machine after WWII; Shepard founded Intelligent Machines Research Corp in 1952 to commercialize it

sources.title: David H. Shepard
sources.quote: In 1952 he formed Intelligent Machines Research Corporation to commercialize the invention with William Lawless Jr. in Arlington, Virginia.

note: Date is a latest bound (Gismo built earlier, undated). Earlier: Tauschek and Goldberg 1929-31 optical-code readers, Goldberg 1915 patent, Optophone 1914 (read letters to the blind) are analogues that don't convert characters to data for computers.

what: US Post Office put the first high-speed optical character reader into operation for preliminary mail sorting

sources.title: Mail sorting
sources.quote: In 1965, the postal service put the first high-speed optical character reader into operation that could handle a preliminary sort automatically.

note: Earlier practical use likely: Shepard's Farrington B reader for credit-card slips ('first major industry use of OCR', undated) and 1950s commercial readers. Detroit detail not confirmed.

what: Creeper, an experimental self-replicating program by Bob Thomas (BBN), moved between PDP-10s over ARPANET; Reaper antivirus followed in 1972

sources.title: Computer virus
sources.quote: Creeper was an experimental self-replicating program written by Bob Thomas at BBN Technologies in 1971.

note: Earlier: von Neumann's 1949 theory of self-reproducing automata (theory only), MIT student phone and computer hacking 1959-63 (The Tech 1963, no actual break-in source), Equity Funding data fraud from 1964 (insider fraud). Later: Elk Cloner 1982, Brain 1986.

what: Morris worm spread across the Internet, disabling many machines

sources.title: Morris worm
sources.quote: The Morris worm or Internet worm of November 2, 1988, was a malicious self-replicating computer program that affected VAX computers

note: Earlier real-world attacks: Elk Cloner (1982, floppy virus in the wild), Brain (1986), Equity Funding records fraud from 1964 (insiders). Chose the first widely disruptive network attack; earlier smaller incidents likely exist.

what: Trinity, the first nuclear test (New Mexico): recording instruments were paralyzed by pickup at the moment of the explosion despite double shielding of signal lines; the effect was later attributed to the nuclear EMP.

sources.title: Nuclear electromagnetic pulse
sources.quote: In spite of this many records were lost because of spurious pickup at the time of the explosion that paralyzed the recording equipment.

sources.title: Nuclear electromagnetic pulse
sources.quote: During the first United States nuclear test on 16 July 1945, electronic equipment was shielded because Enrico Fermi expected the electromagnetic pulse.

note: The quoted technical-history line is quoted via Wikipedia, not read in the original report. Considered later events: British 1952-53 tests ('radioflash' instrument failures), Hardtack Yucca 1958 (first openly reported high-altitude EMP observation), Starfish Prime 1962 (damage to civilian electronics in Hawaii, the first pass choice). Starfish Prime is the first damage to ordinary electrical equipment and first public awareness, but Trinity is the earliest case of electronic equipment disabled by nuclear EMP. Attribution of the 1945 losses to EMP is retrospective, hence medium. Hardening: the 1945 shielding was an early precaution; no distinct first_practical_use or mass_adoption event sourced.

what: Bell Labs' Audrey, built by Balashek, Biddulph and Davis, recognized spoken digits from a single speaker.

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1952 – Bell Labs researchers, Stephen Balashek, R. Biddulph, and K. H. Davis, built Audrey for single-speaker digit recognition.

sources.title: speech recognition (Q189436)
sources.quote: start time (P580): 1952

note: Earlier candidate: Radio Rex (Elmwood Button Co., 1922), a toy dog that leaps out of its house when its name is called. Rejected: it is triggered by acoustic energy near 500 Hz (the vowel in 'Rex'), not by recognizing words, so it is a sound-triggered switch; I also could not fetch a source page for it. Other candidates: RCA 1956 Olson-Belar syllable recognizer, IBM Shoebox 1962 (16 words), all later. Voice-operated doors/locks: no earlier working example found.

what: The Apricot Portable shipped with voice-command recognition (up to 4096 words, 64 in RAM at a time).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1984 – the Apricot Portable was released with up to 4096 words support, of which only 64 could be held in RAM at a time.

note: Wikipedia lists the Apricot Portable first under 'Practical products'. Earlier commercial use likely exists: Threshold Technology's VIP-100 (about 1972, used for factory quality-control data entry), reported by secondary sources I could not fetch. Reject 1987 Kurzweil and 1990 DragonDictate as later. Treat 1984 as an upper bound; true first use is probably early 1970s.

what: Apple launched the iPhone 4S with Siri, putting spoken commands in the hands of ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

note: The first pass gave 2011-10-04, which is the announcement; the iPhone 4S went on sale 14 October 2011. Earlier but narrower mass uses: telephone call-routing by voice (AT&T 1992), DragonDictate/NaturallySpeaking for PC users (1990s) were niche, not routine for ordinary people.

what: IBM's Tangora, a voice-activated typewriter handling a 20,000-word vocabulary, built by Fred Jelinek's team.

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: By the mid-1980s, Fred Jelinek's team at IBM created a voice-activated typewriter called Tangora, which could handle a 20,000-word vocabulary.

note: Year is only 'mid-1980s' in the source; 1985 is an approximation. Almost certainly too late: RCA's Olson and Belar built an experimental 'phonetic typewriter' that typed from speech and published it in J. Acoust. Soc. Am. in 1956 (found via search; I could not fetch a page to quote, so not used). That earlier prototype, limited to a single talker and a small phoneme set, is the likely true first demonstration.

what: Dragon Dictate released as a consumer dictation product (discrete words, DOS).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1990 – Dragon Dictate, a consumer product released in 1990.

note: First pass said 1997 NaturallySpeaking, which was the first continuous-speech product, not the first dictation product. The same Wikipedia list gives 1987 'a recognizer from Kurzweil Applied Intelligence' (Kurzweil's medical-report dictation system); the line has no detail, so I could not confirm it as dictation and kept 1990. An earlier 1987 or 1984-85 product may fit. No mass_adoption sourced: dictation by speech only became routine on smartphones in the 2010s, but no fetched source states it.

what: Wolfgang von Kempelen's bellows-operated acoustic-mechanical speech machine, with models of tongue and lips producing vowels and consonants, described in a 1791 paper.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: There followed the bellows-operated "acoustic-mechanical speech machine" of Wolfgang von Kempelen of Pressburg, Hungary, described in a 1791 paper.

sources.title: Wolfgang von Kempelen
sources.quote: Kempelen also created a manually operated speaking machine.

note: Date is the publication of his description; he worked on the machine for about twenty years before, so a working demonstration probably came earlier (the same page gives 1789 for his book, so sources conflict). Earlier candidate: Kratzenstein 1779, vocal-tract models producing five vowels only, rejected as not producing speech. Later: Voder 1939 (first electronic, human-operated, shown at the New York World's Fair), Kelly-Gerstman IBM 7090 computer synthesis 1961, Umeda's English text-to-speech 1968. The machine was hand-operated, as was the Voder.

what: Telesensory Systems' Speech+ talking calculator for the blind, with a synthesized voice, was in use; the Kurzweil Reading Machine for the Blind (Votrax synthesizer) appeared in the same year.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: One of the first was the Telesensory Systems Inc. (TSI) Speech+ portable calculator for the blind in 1976.

note: Earlier systems existed (Umeda's 1968 text-to-speech, MUSA 1975 reading Italian) but I found no evidence they were used outside the lab. Voder (1939) and Kempelen's machine were exhibitions. Date 1976 is the source's year for 'one of the first' handheld devices; a slightly earlier use is possible.

what: Siri on the iPhone 4S brought a talking computer that answers aloud to ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

note: Judgment call. Earlier mass-market talking devices: Texas Instruments Speak & Spell (1978) and talking games and chess computers (1979-80), which had voices but little routine use as 'answering computers'. Wikipedia source supports the date of launch, not the synthesis itself.

what: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA, developed at MIT 1964-67 and first published in 1966, held typed English conversations by pattern matching.

sources.title: Chatbot
sources.quote: Joseph Weizenbaum's program ELIZA was first published in 1966.

sources.title: ELIZA
sources.quote: ELIZA is an early natural language processing computer program developed from 1964 to 1967 at MIT by Joseph Weizenbaum.

note: ELIZA gives the illusion of understanding (the author said so), so the fit to 'understanding questions' is partial; I kept it as the earliest program that held a conversation. Earlier question-answering programs (BASEBALL, 1961; SAD SAM, 1957) answered narrow questions without dialogue and I did not source them. Later: SHRDLU 1970, PARRY 1972. First pass month 1966-01 is not confirmed by a fetched source, so only the year is given.

what: OpenAI released ChatGPT; it reached 100 million users in two months.

sources.title: ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

note: Earlier mass-market assistants (Siri 2011, Alexa 2014) took commands and short questions rather than holding conversations; chatbots such as SmarterChild (2001) were popular but I did not source them. No first_practical_use is given: no fetched source identifies an out-of-lab deployment before the 1990s and I could not settle it.

what: Georgetown University and IBM translated more than sixty Russian sentences into English automatically on an IBM 701.

sources.title: Georgetown-IBM experiment
sources.quote: The Georgetown–IBM experiment was an influential demonstration of machine translation, which was performed on January 7, 1954.

sources.title: Machine translation
sources.quote: A demonstration was made in 1954 on the APEXC machine at Birkbeck College

note: The 1954 Birkbeck APEXC demonstration (rudimentary English to French; day not given) is the same year and I cannot tell which came first, so the Georgetown date is kept. Mid-1930s patents by Artsrouni (mechanical bilingual dictionary on punched tape) and Troyanskii were proposals or a word-lookup aid, not demonstrated translation. The system was a small demonstration (250 words, six rules).

what: IBM's Automatic Language Translator (AN/GSQ-16) was installed at the US Air Force Foreign Technology Division to convert Soviet technical documents to English.

sources.title: AN/GSQ-16 Automatic Language Translator
sources.quote: The translator was installed in 1959, dramatically upgraded in 1964, and was eventually replaced by a mainframe running SYSTRAN in 1970.

note: Single Wikipedia source. Another source (a 1997 NAIC paper, found by search, not fetched) says the Mark II system was installed at Wright-Patterson in 1964 as one of the first operational MT systems, so the 1959 installation may have been a pre-operational version. Other early uses I did not verify: Georgetown/Euratom/Atomic Energy Commission systems in the early 1960s; METEO weather-bulletin translation (1970s).

what: AltaVista Babel Fish (SYSTRAN) offered free web translation to the public and handled about 500,000 requests a day.

sources.title: Machine translation
sources.quote: AltaVista Babelfish, which racked up 500,000 requests a day (1997)

note: First free web translation was SYSTRAN's 1996 offering; 1997 is when it reached large daily use. Google Translate (April 2006) later brought it to hundreds of millions. 'Routine' use by ordinary people is arguable for 1997; a later date (2006) could also be argued.

what: Marian Rejewski's 'bomba kryptologiczna', an electrically driven aggregate of six Enigma machines at the Polish Cipher Bureau, designed about October 1938 and ready in mid-November 1938.

sources.title: Bomba (cryptography)
sources.quote: In mid-November 1938, the bombs were ready, and the reconstructing of daily keys now took about two hours.

sources.title: Bomba (cryptography)
sources.quote: invented the "bomba kryptologiczna" (cryptologic bomb), probably in October 1938

note: Earlier candidate: the Polish cyclometer (designed 'probably in 1934 or 1935'), which catalogued cycle structures of Enigma permutations to speed decryption. Rejected as the first because it prepared a catalogue rather than testing keys itself, though it arguably also fits 'analysing patterns'. The British Bombe (1940), Heath Robinson (1943) and Colossus (Mark 1 first attacked a message on 5 February 1944) are later; the first pass named Colossus. Before 1938 the Poles used hand 'grill' methods. Pre-electromechanical cryptanalytic machines (e.g. punched-card tabulator aids in the 1930s) were not checked.

what: The Polish bombs were put to use reconstructing the daily Enigma keys at the Cipher Bureau from mid-November 1938.

sources.title: Bomba (cryptography)
sources.quote: In mid-November 1938, the bombs were ready, and the reconstructing of daily keys now took about two hours.

note: Same event as the demonstration: the machines were built for real traffic and operated at the Cipher Bureau, and the source says six were built before September 1939. The page does not quote messages broken on a given day, so 'practical use' rests on the stated purpose. Later pure-practical dates: British Bombe 1940, Colossus 1944.

what: John Clark's Eureka, a mechanical machine that generated Latin hexameter verses automatically (about one a minute), was exhibited at the Egyptian Hall, London, after being built 1830-1845.

sources.title: The Eureka
sources.quote: named John Clark, who then exhibited his invention in the Egyptian Hall in London.

note: Mechanical, not a computer; it fits 'composes poems automatically' but a strict reading of 'a computer' would give Christopher Strachey's love-letter generator on the Ferranti Mark 1 / Manchester Mark 1 (1952), the first computer-generated literature, which is the first pass candidate (the first pass said 1953; sources give summer 1952, one gives 1953). Eureka's method was the published 1677 scheme of John Peter, but Clark fully automated it. Build dates: 1830-1843 (some sources) or 1845. Shannon's 1948 Markov text examples were hand-made and not considered.

what: Environment Canada deployed FoG, which generated weather forecasts in English and French from data automatically.

sources.title: Natural-language generation
sources.quote: The earliest such system to be deployed was FoG, which was used by Environment Canada to generate weather forecasts

note: Source says only 'early 1990s'; 1990 is a placeholder year. Literature I recall gives about 1992 but I did not source it. Later: Reuters Tracer and the Associated Press / Los Angeles Times Quakebot (2014). Earlier practical text generation (e.g. form-letter mail merge) is a template fill, not composition. Eureka (1845) was a paid exhibition, not a practical tool.

what: ChatGPT made automatic writing of text available to ordinary users, reaching 100 million users in two months.

sources.title: ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

note: Earlier mass exposure was to machine-written news snippets (AP earnings and sports reports since 2014) that readers did not choose or operate; ChatGPT is when ordinary people used machine writing routinely themselves.

what: CSIRAC, Australia's first computer (Trevor Pearcey and Maston Beard, CSIRO, Sydney), was programmed to play music, the first known use of a digital computer for the purpose.

sources.title: CSIRAC
sources.quote: In 1950 CSIRAC was used to play music, the first known use of a digital computer for the purpose.

sources.title: Computer music
sources.quote: The world's first computer to play music was the CSIR Mark 1

note: Fits 'performs music' (playing popular melodies programmed by Geoff Hill) but the music was not composed by the machine. Strachey's Ferranti Mark 1 national anthem in late 1951 is later (first recording). Composition by computer: Illiac Suite (1957; Hiller and Isaacson), 'generally agreed to be the first score composed by an electronic computer', so 'composes' dates to 1956-57. Art: Desmond Paul Henry's drawing machine (1961, adapted analogue bombsight computer), Michael Noll 1962, AARON (from 1972); Ben Laposky's 1950 analogue 'oscillons' were not checked. Earlier automata (Jaquet-Droz 1770s, al-Jazari) replay fixed mechanisms and I excluded them. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: the sources found do not mark out a use outside the lab, and AI image generators of 2022 are described only as approaching human quality, not adoption.

what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC at Princeton (funding summer 1951), a neural-net machine that learned by reinforcement to solve a maze.

sources.title: Stochastic neural analog reinforcement calculator
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

note: Candidates: Ashby's Homeostat (1948, adapts to disturbances; closer to self-regulation than learning from experience), Shannon's Theseus maze mouse (1950; relays remember the maze path, and whether it 'learned' is disputed), Samuel's checkers program (begun 1949, first ran 1952, paper 1959; 'machine learning' coined 1959) and Rosenblatt's perceptron (1957-58). SNARC is a simulated maze solved by reinforced weights, so I take it as the earliest clear case, but this is a judgment and the date is only the year. Page for Theseus could not be fetched. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: ADALINE (1960) adaptive filters and later uses were not sourced, and 'routine' consumer use is too diffuse to date.

what: The first programs that could play a full game of standard chess were written, by Alex Bernstein (IBM 704) and by Russian programmers on a BESM.

sources.title: Computer chess
sources.quote: The first programs that can play a full game of chess are developed, one by Alex Bernstein and one by Russian programmers

note: Earlier candidates and why rejected: El Ajedrecista (Torres Quevedo, 1912), an electromechanical machine playing only king and rook against king (not a program or computer); Turing's Turochamp (1948-52), never run on a computer, played by hand in 1952; Prinz's 1951 Ferranti Mark 1 program, which only solved mate-in-two problems; Los Alamos chess on MANIAC I (1956), the first chess-like game played by a computer program but on a 6x6 board without bishops, a variant, not chess. If the variant counts, 1956 is the answer. Strict reading used here.

what: Fidelity Electronics released Chess Challenger, the first dedicated chess computer sold to the public.

sources.title: Computer chess
sources.quote: In March, Fidelity Electronics releases Chess Challenger, the first dedicated chess computer to be sold.

note: Practical use taken as sale to people who play chess with it. Chess programs ran in the ACM computer chess championships from 1970, but that is competition between programs, not a product. Superhuman level (Deep Blue beating Kasparov, 1997) is not a listed kind. No mass_adoption date is sourced.

what: Westinghouse's Nimatron, an electromechanical relay machine conceived by Edward Condon, played Nim against fairgoers at the New York World's Fair.

sources.title: Nimatron
sources.quote: It was first exhibited in April–October 1940 by the Westinghouse Electric Corporation at the 1939-1940 New York World's Fair to entertain fair-goers.

note: Replaces the first pass's Strachey draughts program (1951-52) and the Nimrod machine (1951), both later. Chess-only machines (El Ajedrecista, 1912) belong to the chess concept. Earlier ideas (Babbage's planned tic-tac-toe automaton, 1840s) were never built. The month is the opening of the 1940 season of the fair; the build was done in the months before.

what: The Nimatron was in public use at the fair as entertainment, with about 100,000 games of Nim played against visitors.

sources.title: Nimatron
sources.quote: The reception of the machine during the fair was positive, with around 100,000 games of Nim played.

note: Same event as the demonstration: the purpose of the machine was to entertain fairgoers, so public exhibition is its real use. No mass_adoption event sourced for game-playing programs as a category.

what: Larry Roberts's MIT PhD thesis 'Machine Perception of Three-Dimensional Solids' (block-world scene analysis from camera images).

sources.title: Lawrence Roberts
sources.quote: Machine Perception of Three-Dimensional Solids

note: Source supports the thesis and 1963 PhD, 'father of computer vision'; the quote does not itself describe the demo. Earlier pattern-recognition/photoelectric-eye work (1950s) not searched successfully. Navigation by vision (Shakey, 1966-72) is later.

what: Research on electronic noses (Persaud and Dodd, Warwick, Nature 1982) began.

sources.title: Electronic nose
sources.quote: Since 1982, research has been conducted to develop technologies, commonly referred to as electronic noses

note: Quote supports only the 1982 start of e-nose research. Earlier tactile sensors for robots/prostheses (1960s-70s) and Moncrieff's 1961 mechanical odour sensor likely earlier but unverified.

what: Griffith P. Taylor built a Meccano programmable crane robot (punched-tape controlled, five axes) that stacked blocks; published in Meccano Magazine, March 1938.

sources.title: Industrial robot
sources.quote: The earliest known industrial robot conforming to the ISO definition was completed by

note: Fits the ISO definition mechanically but is a hobby model that did no factory work, so it is weak as a demonstration of factory labour. Unimate prototype (c.1958-60) and Roselund/DeVilbiss spray-painting patents (1938-42) considered; could not fetch sources for them (only Wikipedia reachable).

what: First Unimate installed at GM Inland Fisher Guide plant, Ewing Township NJ, lifting hot die-cast parts.

sources.title: Unimate
sources.quote: which worked on a General Motors assembly line at the Inland Fisher Guide Plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, in 1961

sources.title: Unimation
sources.quote: In 1960, Devol personally sold the first Unimate robot, which was shipped in 1961 to General Motors.

note: Some sources (Automate.org, not fetchable here) say a prototype was installed at GM Trenton in 1959; unverified. DeVilbiss painting robot (1940s) has no verified deployment.

what: Fanuc's robot plant near Mount Fuji runs lights-out, robots building robots, unsupervised for up to 30 days.

sources.title: Lights out (manufacturing)
sources.quote: FANUC, a Japanese robotics company, has been a lights-out factory since 2001.

note: First pass cited a 1981 report of Fanuc unattended operation (16 hours a day); I could not verify it, so a much earlier event likely exists. Date here is the latest-source date only.

what: Unimation, called the world's first robotics company, shipped its first Unimate to General Motors.

sources.title: Unimation
sources.quote: Unimation was the world's first robotics company

sources.title: Unimation
sources.quote: In 1960, Devol personally sold the first Unimate robot, which was shipped in 1961 to General Motors.

note: First commercial robot sale/delivery. Founding date is inconsistent (Wikipedia says 1962; first pass said 1956). Mass-production and repair aspects of the definition not separately dated.

what: Westinghouse's Elektro (built 1937-38) shown at the 1939 New York World's Fair; walked by voice command, spoke about 700 words, moved head and arms.

sources.title: Elektro
sources.quote: he could walk by voice command, speak about 700 words

sources.title: Elektro
sources.quote: Elektro was on exhibit at the 1939 New York World's Fair

note: Earlier than first-pass WABOT-1 (1973), but Elektro was largely remote-scripted and did not handle objects in the human sense; fit is loose. Eric (1928) and WABOT-1 pages could not be verified.

what: Disney's Audio-Animatronic Abraham Lincoln shown in 'Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln' at the Illinois pavilion, 1964 New York World's Fair

sources.title: Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln
sources.quote: Originally created by Walt Disney for the State of Illinois pavilion at the 1964 New York World's Fair

note: A figure of one particular (dead) person; it is a likeness rather than a verified exact double. Rejected as later: Repliee Q1Expo (2005) and Geminoid HI-1 (2006, Ishiguro's copy of himself, teleoperated). Earlier wax or automaton portraits not found as robots.

what: Whirlpool demonstrated a track-following robotic floor sweeper concept (Donald Moore's 1957 patent) at the American National Exhibition in Moscow

sources.title: Robotic vacuum cleaner
sources.quote: Whirlpool demonstrated the concept at the 1959 American National Exhibition but did not bring it to market.

note: Follows a track under the floor, so only a loose fit to 'on its own'. Later: MowBot 1969, Electrolux Trilobite 1996, Roomba 2002. Heinlein 1956 was fiction.

what: MowBot, autonomous robotic lawn mower patented by S. Lawrence Bellinger, sold for about $800

sources.title: Robotic lawn mower
sources.quote: In 1969, the MowBot was introduced and patented by S Lawrence Bellinger having many features of today's most popular products.

note: No earlier robot mower or vacuum on sale found in the pages read. Trilobite (1996) and Roomba (2002) are later. Whether MowBot was truly autonomous rests on this one source.

what: Coin-operated brass tobacco dispensers operated in English taverns

sources.title: Vending machine
sources.quote: Coin-operated machines that dispensed tobacco were being operated as early as 1615 in the taverns of England.

note: Considered and rejected as later: Carlile newspaper machine 1822, Denham stamp machine 1867, Everitt postcard machine 1883, Quisisana automat Berlin 1895, Horn & Hardart Philadelphia 1902. The 1615 claim is from one reference page without a primary source.

what: Coin-operated postcard and stationery machines, introduced in London in 1883, became widespread at railway stations and post offices

sources.title: Vending machine
sources.quote: soon became a widespread feature at railway stations and post offices

note: Exact year of becoming common not given; 1883 is the introduction. Automats became popular in New York after 1912 (Horn & Hardart).

what: Sony introduced the first consumer AIBO robot dog (ERS-110)

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: The first consumer model was introduced on 11 May 1999 and was followed by updated generations.

note: Companionship fit is loose (AIBO means pal). Paro was designed from 1993 but first shown to the public in late 2001 per the page read (first pass said 1998, not confirmed). No romance or sex robot (RealDoll 1997 is a doll, not a robot; Realbotix 2018) earlier.

what: AIBO ERS-110 went on sale and sold out in 20 minutes

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: Sales began on 1 June 1999 and sold out via the Internet in 20 minutes.

note: Paro handmade versions sold from 2004 are later.

what: W. Grey Walter's tortoise robots Elmer and Elsie in Bristol, built 1948-1949

sources.title: Grey Walter
sources.quote: Elmer and Elsie, were constructed between 1948 and 1949

note: Earlier candidates: Hammond and Miessner's Electric Dog (c. 1912, a light-seeking prop; the page read gives no date for it); Vaucanson's duck (1739, page read gives wrong date); ancient and medieval animal automata (Hellenistic, Al-Jazari). Not dated from sources I could fetch, so 1948 may be too late.

what: Tiger Electronics released the Furby, an electronic robotic toy creature, in October 1998

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: Originally released in October 1998

note: Furby is a creature toy rather than a dog or cat, but sold as a pet-like robot. Considered: AIBO ERS-110 sales 1 June 1999 (later, higher fidelity as robot dog); Teddy Ruxpin 1985 (talking animated bear, not pet-like).

what: Furby sold 14 million units in 1999 after 1.8 million in 1998

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: with 1.8 million sold in 1998 and 14 million in 1999

note: Toy-store scale adoption. AIBO sold only thousands in 1999.

what: Key-wound spring-driven clockwork monk, now in the Smithsonian, possibly dating as early as 1560

sources.title: Automaton
sources.quote: The monk is driven by a key-wound spring and walks the path of a square, striking his chest

note: Date is 'possibly'. Earlier automata rejected on mechanism (water, weights, pneumatics): Hellenistic (Ktesibios, Hero), Al-Jazari 1206, Strasbourg clock figures (14th c.). Leonardo's mechanical lion and knight (c. 1495-1515) may have been spring or weight driven; unclear.

what: Knightscope shipped its first autonomous security patrol robot

sources.title: Knightscope
sources.quote: Knightscope shipped their first robot in 2015.

note: Almost certainly too late. Earlier: Denning Sentry (mid-1980s), ROBART I (c. 1982), PROWLER armed sentry (developed from 1983); I could not fetch usable dated sources for them.

what: US Navy testing of pre-production Mark 24 'FIDO' acoustic homing torpedoes, which steer themselves onto a target

sources.title: Mark 24 mine
sources.quote: Testing of the pre-production prototypes continued into December 1942

note: Date is when prototype tests were still running; the first successful test date is not given. Naval and land mines considered and rejected: they do not find targets. Phalanx CIWS (OT&E 1977) is later.

what: Mark 24 mine entered Allied service in March 1943; first U-boat kills claimed in May 1943

sources.title: Mark 24 mine
sources.quote: Two engagements in May 1943 have a claim for the first U-boat sunk by FIDO.

note: German G7es acoustic torpedo also entered service in 1943. Kargu-2 (2020) is far later.

what: Lt. John Dumaresq, Royal Navy, invented the Dumaresq, a mechanical analog computer relating own-ship and target motion for gunnery

sources.title: Dumaresq
sources.quote: The Dumaresq is a mechanical calculating device invented around 1902 by Lieutenant John Dumaresq of the Royal Navy.

note: It computes relative motion (range rate), not full aim; Dreyer Table and Ford Rangekeeper (1916) came later. Missile guidance (V-1, V-2, Fritz X, 1940s) not searched and later in any case.

what: Mechanical fire-control aids such as the Dumaresq began to be available to the Royal Navy around 1905

sources.title: Fire-control system
sources.quote: Around 1905, mechanical fire control aids began to become available

note: Dumaresq patented August 1904 and about 1000 bought by 1913. Rangekeeper 1916 (first pass) is later.

what: SAGE air-defence computers (IBM AN/FSQ-7) became operational in the late 1950s

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: SAGE became operational in the late 1950s and early 1960s

note: Air-defence tracking, not war planning. Earlier candidates not verifiable here: Army Operations Research Office computer war-game and combat simulations (Air Defense Simulation 1948, Carmonette 1953) seen only in search summaries; ORO founded 1948. Likely earlier events exist.

what: Walgreens installed a Kiva mobile-robot fulfilment system at Mount Vernon, Illinois

sources.title: Amazon Robotics
sources.quote: Walgreens installed one at its distribution center in Mount Vernon, Illinois, in 2007

note: Too late probably: AGV fleets under central computer traffic control existed in the 1970s (Volvo Kalmar 1972-74 seen only in search summaries, central control not confirmed). Staples 2006 not confirmed.

what: Raymond Goertz at Argonne National Laboratory built and patented a bilateral master-slave manipulator for handling radioactive material through a hot-cell window.

sources.title: Raymond Goertz
sources.quote: In 1949, while working for the Atomic Energy Commission at Argonne National Laboratory, Goertz filed a patent for an early master-slave manipulator

sources.title: Raymond Goertz
sources.quote: The initial master-slave manipulator device was designed by Goertz in 1948 as a seven-degree-of-freedom bilateral (symmetrical) metal tape transmission pantograph device

note: Design dated 1948, patent filed 1949; no fetched page gives the date of the first working demonstration. Earlier Torres Quevedo Telekino (1903) was remote control without the operator seeing or feeling through the machine; rejected. GE/Payne 1948 device not verified.

what: Modified Goertz master-slave manipulator (CRL Model 8) went into commercial production for nuclear remote handling.

sources.title: Raymond Goertz
sources.quote: by 1954 a modified version of the master-slave manipulator (CRL Model 8) began commercial production

note: Argonne likely used earlier models in hot cells from about 1949-51 but no fetched source dates that; 1954 is a later bound only.

what: Luna 1 (USSR), launched 2 Jan 1959, left Earth orbit, passed the Moon and became the first spacecraft in solar orbit, returning data.

sources.title: Luna 1
sources.quote: was the first spacecraft to reach the vicinity of Earth's Moon, the first spacecraft to leave Earth's orbit

note: Considered Sputnik 1 and Explorer 1 (Earth-orbit satellites, not another body or deep space) and rejected them. Earlier Pioneer 0/1 attempts failed. Deep-sea robot probes not found in fetchable sources.

what: Stoddart's rotaxane molecular shuttle, the breakthrough in synthesising artificial molecular machines (first reported working example 1994 in same article).

sources.title: Molecular machine
sources.quote: the actual breakthrough in practical approaches to synthesize artificial molecular machines (AMMs) took place in 1991 with the invention of a "molecular shuttle"

note: Molecular-scale machine only; no robot working inside the body exists, so no first_practical_use or mass_adoption. Sauvage catenane 1983 considered, a structure not a machine. The first pass cited 2004-2010 DNA walkers, which are later.

what: Hideo Kodama (Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute) published methods and results for building 3D plastic models layer by layer from photo-hardening polymer.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: His research results as journal papers were published in April and November 1981.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: In April 1980, Hideo Kodama of Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute invented two additive methods for fabricating three-dimensional plastic models

note: Earlier than Hull's 1984 patent. Raytheon 1982 layered-powder patent is later. Whether Kodama's design was driven by a digital design file is not stated; fit is on layer-by-layer automatic building.

what: 3D Systems, co-founded by Chuck Hull, commercialised stereolithography (first machine, SLA-1, reported 1987).

sources.title: Stereolithography
sources.quote: After the patent was granted in 1986, Hull co-founded the world's first 3D printing company, 3D Systems, to commercialize it.

note: Quote supports commercialisation after 1986 only; the 1987 SLA-1 date comes from the first pass and was not fetched. No mass_adoption established (consumer RepRap era 2005+ not sourced as routine use).

what: Francois Willeme's photosculpture: photographs taken in the round used to reproduce a person as a 3D sculpture.

sources.title: Photosculpture
sources.quote: The process was invented and patented by French artist (painter, sculptor and photographer) François Willème in 1860.

note: Records the full shape of an object for reproduction, but optically and not digitally. Ferranti's 1950s coordinate-measuring machine measures points only and is not for reproduction; Cyberware 1984 head scanner from first pass could not be sourced.

what: Lawrence Sperry demonstrated the Sperry gyroscopic autopilot in Paris (flying hands off the controls); system developed 1912.

sources.title: Autopilot
sources.quote: Lawrence Sperry, the son of famous inventor Elmer Sperry, demonstrated it in 1914 at an aviation safety contest held in Paris.

note: Development in 1912 considered; no dated demonstration found for 1912. Day 1914-06-18 comes from the first pass and was not confirmed.

what: Standard Oil tanker J.A. Moffet became the first ship to use an autopilot (Sperry gyropilot).

sources.title: Autopilot
sources.quote: In the early 1920s, the Standard Oil tanker J.A. Moffet became the first ship to use an autopilot.

note: Year 1922 is from memory of the Moffet installation; source says only early 1920s. Aircraft use: 1930 Army Air Corps three-hour test, 1947 full transatlantic autopilot flight, later than this.

what: Gemini 3 flew with the IBM Gemini guidance computer, controlling mission maneuvers (orbit changes by crew).

sources.title: Gemini Guidance Computer
sources.quote: The computer, which facilitated the control of mission maneuvers, was designed by the IBM Federal Systems Division.

sources.title: Gemini 3
sources.quote: It was the first U.S. mission in which the crew fired thrusters to change the size and shape of their orbit

note: Earlier than the first pass (Apollo 1968). That Gemini 3 carried the computer is from background knowledge, not a fetched sentence. Missile and submarine inertial guidance computers (late 1950s) not checked.

what: Same flight: first operational use of an onboard computer for orbital maneuvers on a crewed spacecraft.

sources.title: Gemini Guidance Computer
sources.quote: The computer, which facilitated the control of mission maneuvers, was designed by the IBM Federal Systems Division.

note: Same event as the demonstration; see note there.

what: Tsukuba Mechanical Engineering Laboratory (Japan) vehicle drove itself at up to 30 km/h using two cameras to detect street markings.

sources.title: History of self-driving cars
sources.quote: In 1977, the first self-driving car that operated independently of wires under the road was designed by the Japanese Tsukuba Mechanical Engineering Laboratory.

note: 1950s wire-guided cars (RCA/GM) and 1920s radio-controlled cars considered; they follow buried wire or have a remote operator, so rejected. Dickmanns 1987 is later. No fully driverless public service verified (Waymo One Dec 2018 was remotely monitored), so no practical use.

what: A. M. Low's radio-controlled de Havilland monoplane flew under control in Britain.

sources.title: Unmanned aerial vehicle
sources.quote: Low confirmed that Geoffrey de Havilland's monoplane was the one that flew under control on 21 March 1917 using his radio system.

note: Hewitt-Sperry Automatic Airplane flew about 1,000 yards controlled on 1918-03-06 (Wikipedia: first unmanned heavier-than-air controlled flight); Low's claim is disputed and earlier than that. 1849 Austrian balloons are unpowered, rejected.

what: DJI Phantom, an affordable ready-to-fly consumer drone, launched in 2013 and opened the consumer drone market.

sources.title: Unmanned aerial vehicle
sources.quote: The DJI Phantom was considered one of the most influential consumer drone products ever made.

note: Year of launch of the product that started mass consumer use, not a measured usage figure. First practical use (1920s-30s target drones such as Fairey Queen, Queen Bee) not dated by a fetched source.

what: Skylab launched with an onboard digital computer controlling its attitude and pointing.

sources.title: Skylab
sources.quote: The mission computer used aboard Skylab was the IBM System/4Pi TC-1, a relative of the AP-101 Space Shuttle computers.

sources.title: Skylab
sources.quote: Skylab was launched on May 14, 1973, by the modified Saturn V.

note: Sources show an onboard computer for attitude control only, not life support. Salyut 1 (1971) computers not found in fetchable sources, so an earlier event may exist.

what: UNIVAC I, used by CBS on election night, predicted an Eisenhower landslide from 5.5% of the vote.

sources.title: UNIVAC I
sources.quote: The fifth machine (built for the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission) was used by CBS to predict the result of the 1952 presidential election.

note: Earlier computer forecasts not found. Statistical model of people, as definition requires; the machine was off on the first try, but the 442 vs 438 electoral vote result was close.

what: Same broadcast: the forecast was used on live television for the real election.

sources.title: UNIVAC I
sources.quote: On election night, Eisenhower received 34,075,029 votes in a 442–89 Electoral College victory. UNIVAC had a margin of error of 3.5%

note: Same event as the demonstration. Computerized predictions then became a widely used part of election night broadcasts, but no dated source for mass adoption.

what: Chile's Project Cybersyn linked state enterprises by telex to a central mainframe for production monitoring and economic simulation.

sources.title: Project Cybersyn
sources.quote: Project Cybersyn was a Chilean economic project developed from 1971 to 1973 during the socialist presidency of Salvador Allende

note: Date 1972 is from the first pass (October 1972 strike); fetched page gives only 1971-73. USAF Project SCOOP (linear-programming planning on SEAC, about 1951) may be earlier but I could not fetch a source. NYSE DOT (1970s) only routes orders.

what: Joan Ball's St. James Computer Dating Service (later Com-Pat) in London ran its first computer match-ups of questionnaire answers on a time-shared computer.

sources.title: Joan Ball
sources.quote: the bureau ran its first set of computer match ups in 1964.

sources.title: Operation Match
sources.quote: inspired by Joan Ball's St. James Computer Dating Service (later Com-Pat) which started in London in 1964.

note: Considered Operation Match (1965, later), the Scientific Marriage Foundation (1957, IBM card-sorting machine, not a computer, so rejected) and unnamed earlier European computer dating services that Wikipedia says preceded both Com-Pat and Operation Match; I could not identify or date them, so an earlier event may exist. Demonstration and first service are the same event.

what: Joan Ball's St. James Computer Dating Service (later Com-Pat) in London ran its first computer match-ups of questionnaire answers on a time-shared computer.

sources.title: Joan Ball
sources.quote: the bureau ran its first set of computer match ups in 1964.

sources.title: Operation Match
sources.quote: inspired by Joan Ball's St. James Computer Dating Service (later Com-Pat) which started in London in 1964.

note: Considered Operation Match (1965, later), the Scientific Marriage Foundation (1957, IBM card-sorting machine, not a computer, so rejected) and unnamed earlier European computer dating services that Wikipedia says preceded both Com-Pat and Operation Match; I could not identify or date them, so an earlier event may exist. Demonstration and first service are the same event.

what: John Horty's Health Law Center at the University of Pittsburgh built a computer database of statutes searchable by computer, shown to the American Bar Association in 1960.

sources.title: University of Pittsburgh School of Law
sources.quote: During the 1950s and 1960s, the School of Law's Health Law Center was an early pioneer in the field now known as computer-assisted legal research

note: The fetched page says only 1950s-60s; the 1960 ABA demonstration year comes from a search-result snippet I could not fetch (non-Wikipedia sites were blocked by the proxy). Only the legal-research part of the definition is real; no computer issues verdicts or warrants.

what: Mead Data Central publicly launched LEXIS in New York as a commercial computerized legal research service for lawyers.

sources.title: LexisNexis
sources.quote: On April 2, 1973, MDC publicly launched LEXIS at a press conference in New York City

note: Earlier candidates: Horty's Pittsburgh system (1960s) and the Ohio Bar's OBAR (contract 1967, per the same article), which were in use before LEXIS but whose first service dates I could not source. LEXIS is the first commercial end-user service. No verdict or sentencing milestone exists.

what: The FBI's National Crime Information Center, a computerized national database of wanted persons and stolen property, was created.

sources.title: National Crime Information Center
sources.quote: The NCIC database was created in 1967 under FBI director J. Edgar Hoover.

note: Loose fit: NCIC looks up records to find wanted people but does not analyse evidence or predict crime. Search results suggested city police computers (e.g. St. Louis, c.1965) pre-date NCIC but I could not fetch a source. PredPol (2011) is a later, predictive-policing event; no earlier predictive milestone was verified.

what: IBM mechanized voting and ballot tabulation for single transferable vote elections, with voters recording preferences on punched cards by dial machine.

sources.title: Voting machine
sources.quote: By July 1936, IBM had mechanized voting and ballot tabulation for single transferable vote elections.

note: Electromechanical rather than computer; whether it was used in a real election is not stated. Considered Edison's 1869 electric vote recorder and legislative electric roll-call devices but could not source them. Lever machines (1892) and McTammany punched-paper machines (1890s) are mechanical, so rejected.

what: Seven US counties switched to punched-card voting with computer tallying for the 1964 presidential election.

sources.title: Electronic voting
sources.quote: Their first widespread use was in the US where 7 counties switched to this method for the 1964 presidential election.

note: The Voting machine article dates the Votomatic's first major success to 1965; the Electronic voting article says 1964. Earlier small-scale uses may exist.

what: By the 1996 US presidential election punched-card systems with computer tabulation were used by over a third of registered US voters.

sources.title: Voting machine
sources.quote: By the 1996 Presidential election, some variation of the punched card system was used by 37.3% of registered voters in the United States.

note: US-only figure; the share may have exceeded this or been similar earlier. Brazil and India adopted DRE machines nationally later.

what: The NSA/GCHQ ECHELON network was formally established to intercept satellite communications and screen them by keyword.

sources.title: Echelon (signals intelligence)
sources.quote: the ECHELON project became formally established in 1971.

sources.title: Echelon (signals intelligence)
sources.quote: US intelligence uses interception systems and keyword searches to monitor European businesses.

note: Weak fit: sources describe keyword screening, not transcription of speech. SHAMROCK (1945-75) handled telegrams largely by hand, so rejected. I found no source for earlier automated speech screening.

what: Harvard researchers (the Schwitzgebel brothers) developed portable transceivers that recorded the location of volunteers.

sources.title: Electronic tagging
sources.quote: Portable transceivers that could record the location of volunteers were first developed by a group of researchers at Harvard University in the early 1960s.

note: Source gives only 'early 1960s'; 1962 is a midpoint, not a sourced year. The first pass said 1964, unverified. Vehicle-tracking and animal/astronaut telemetry were not examined.

what: Judge Jack Love persuaded Michael Goss to found NIMCOS, which built radio ankle transmitters used to monitor offenders from a telephone-linked receiver.

sources.title: Electronic tagging
sources.quote: in 1982, an Arizona state district judge, Jack Love, convinced a former sales representative of Honeywell Information Systems, Michael T. Goss

note: The page gives 1982 for the company; the first pass said the first tagged probationer was in April 1983 (New Mexico), which I could not source. The Schwitzgebel 1960s system was a research use with volunteers.

what: IBM developed a way of attaching magnetic stripes to plastic cards under a US government contract for a security system.

sources.title: Magnetic stripe card
sources.quote: In 1960, IBM built upon the magnetic tape idea and developed a reliable way of securing magnetic stripes to plastic cards

note: The same article says Forrest Parry had the idea in 1969, so 1960 conflicts with it. Punched-card key systems and earlier access cards were not checked.
